newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. calls on Latam to seek more steel markets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls on Latam to seek more steel markets.

text.p: The chairman of the American Iron and Steel Institute called on Latin American nations Monday to promote more steel use to help safeguard the global industry from stiff competition.

Robert J. Grow, also the head of Geneva Steel based in Utah, told the Latin Americn Steel Congress here in northern Mexico, that steel consumption was continually under pressure from other products that were penetrating traditional steel bastions.

"Many products that traditionlly had been made with steel now are made with other materials. Plastic, aluminium, wood, glass, compounds and other materials have usurped steel to a significant degree. This trend must change if we want to continue being part of a growing market," Grow said.

He cited the example of the reduction of the use of steel in cars as one example, adding that the U.S. steel industry had long been aware of the sagging market share, even looking to produce a steel car weighing a third of what autos weigh today through advanced technology called Ultra Light Steel Auto Body, known by the initials ULSAB.
Grow said traditional markets could go the way of steel cans, now largely overtaken by aluminium, if steel producers did not take action to promote their wares.

But he added there were positive lights on the horizon. He said the market for building the shells of houses with steel was growing considerably. "In 1992, U.S. builders reported that 500 houses had been contructed with steel shells. That number jumped to 40,000 in 1994 and should pass 100,000 this year," he said.
Grow said a survey from the National Association of House Builders said 35 percent of members were considering or using steel shells in project this year.
"In Australia, I've been told that practically half the new houses built are using steel. This use of steel in construction is probably the biggest unexplored market in the world," he added.
